entities.name: Ea-mukin-zeri
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ea-mukin-zēri, inscribed as mdÉ-a-mu-kin-NUMUN in cuneiform texts, ascended to the throne of Babylon around 1004 BCE, marking him as the second ruler of the Second Sealand Dynasty, also known as the Fifth Dynasty of Babylon. His brief and contested reign, lasting either three or five months according to divergent ancient chronicles, places him squarely within the turbulent period following the collapse of the Kassite dynasty and preceding the stable Isin II dynasty, a phase often characterized as the "Babylonian Dark Age." His obscure tenure reflects the fragmented political landscape and struggle for centralized authority in southern Mesopotamia during the early first millennium BCE, a critical juncture between the Late Bronze Age collapse and the rise of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

His rule was defined by its brevity and the immediate succession struggles that plagued Babylonia. The Dynastic Chronicle records his reign as a mere three months, while Kinglist A, another vital source for Mesopotamian chronology, extends it to five months. Both accounts agree on his parentage, identifying him as the son of Hašmar, though Hašmar's own identity and role remain largely unclarified, suggesting a non-royal lineage or a regional power base perhaps within the Sealand marshlands. This short duration points to a swift overthrow or an inability to consolidate power against rival claimants or internal factions, typical of the volatile political climate of the era. He succeeded Simbar-šihu, the founder of the Sealand dynasty, suggesting a continuation, albeit unstable, of a new political order emerging from the southern marshes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ea-mukin-zēri's brief and contested reign serves as a crucial, albeit minor, data point in reconstructing the fragmented history of the "Babylonian Dark Age," illustrating the deep political instability and dynastic struggles that characterized early first millennium BCE Mesopotamia.
